reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Monitoring Needs Based on the Project Delivery Method
sections.summary: Fewer, larger, higher resistance piles make construction monitoring critical (less redundancy, tighter tolerances, higher resistance factors); the inspector is the owner's eyes and ears, not just a blow counter, and early detection limits problems. Duties differ between design-bid-build and design-build (Table 18-1); CMGC follows either.
sections.body: 18.1 Monitoring Needs Based on the Project Delivery Method (pp. 447 to 448). Chapter intro: knowledgeable monitoring and inspection are critical, especially as cost effective designs use fewer piles of higher nominal resistance with larger sections and equipment, giving less redundancy, smaller tolerances and higher resistance factors. Monitoring is only as good as the inspector's knowledge, experience and qualifications; inspection is needed for acceptance whatever the delivery method; inspectors must understand their role, the hammer and accessories, pile behavior and soils. Most problems are avoidable with systematic inspection and good communication; the inspector is the 'eyes and ears' of owner and engineer, and early detection and reporting keep problems manageable, while unattended problems spread to more piles and raise costs and claims. Sources: DFI (1995, 1997), Rausche et al. (1986), manufacturers' literature, Florida DOT's manual (Passe 1994). Delivery method: projects were historically design-bid-build (DBB); design-build (DB) and CMGC are increasingly used for faster delivery; Table 18-1 (printed in 18.2) compares agency duties under DBB and DB; CMGC duties follow either depending on the project.
key_points: Fewer, larger piles make construction monitoring critical
The inspector is the owner's eyes and ears, not just a blow counter
Early detection and reporting limit cost, claims and delays
Inspection duties differ between design-bid-build and design-build (Table 18-1)
sections.applicability: The pile inspector's role and how monitoring duties vary with the project delivery method.

sections.title: Items to Be Monitored
sections.summary: Inspector items on every project: review the design report, plans and specifications; inspect piles; review the installation plan; inspect equipment before and during driving; inspect test or indicator piles; inspect production piles and keep records. Table 18-1 lists DBB and DB duties; Figure 18-1 is the inspection flow chart.
sections.body: 18.2 Items to Be Monitored (pp. 448 to 450). Whatever the delivery method, the inspector monitors test piles (for order lengths or load testing) and production piles, grouped as: (1) review of the foundation design report, plans and specifications before arriving; (2) inspection of piles before installation; (3) review of the contractor's pile installation plan; (4) inspection of driving equipment before and during operation; (5) inspection of test or indicator pile installation; (6) inspection during production driving and driving records. Table 18-1 (DBB; DB): installation plan and hammer submittal (review plan and perform or review hammer approval analyses; submit DB team plan to the Engineer for conformance); test pile installation (inspect piles, hammer and appurtenances, record driving, splices, alignment, location, elevation; observe others' installation and documentation); nominal resistance verification (perform observations or tests; review results); driving criteria and order lengths (analyze and establish; review the DB team's); production installation (inspect and record; check piles met the criteria and plan requirements); foundation certification (documentation; review the DB package with the Engineer); verification testing (not applicable; select piles with the Engineer); problems (identify, document, evaluate and coordinate; document resolution). Figure 18-1: the inspection process flow chart; the Contact Engineer is the agency engineer on DBB and the DB team's foundation engineer of record on DB.
key_points: Six inspection areas: documents, piles, installation plan, equipment, test piles, production piles
Table 18-1: agency inspection duties under design-bid-build vs. design-build
Figure 18-1: inspection process flow chart; Contact Engineer depends on delivery method

figures.title: Key components of the pile installation inspection process
figures.description: Flow chart: review plans and specifications; check the hammer and accessories are as approved; check pile type, length and material strength; confirm the driving criteria including minimum penetration; confirm field splicing procedures and inspection requirements; drive test piles to the driving criteria; inspect the hammer in operation; drive production piles to the criteria; check pile location, alignment and heave; prepare the pile installation documentation. Any 'No' leads to Contact Engineer.

tables.title: Overview of Key Construction Monitoring and Inspection Items and Agency Inspection Duties on Design-Bid-Build and Design Build Contracts
tables.description: Agency duties by item for design-bid-build and design-build: pile installation plan and hammer submittal (review plan and hammer approval analyses / submit the DB team's plan for a conformance check); test pile installation (inspect and record / observe others and communicate concerns); resistance verification (perform observations or tests / review results); driving criteria and order lengths (establish / review the DB team's); production piles (inspect and record / check piles met the criteria); foundation certification (documentation / review the DB package); verification testing (not applicable / select piles with the Engineer); piling problems (identify and coordinate resolution / document resolution).

sections.applicability: Items a pile inspector monitors on every project.

sections.title: Review of Project Plans and Specifications
sections.summary: First review the plans and specifications: equipment, procedures, test program and preliminary criteria; know whether the inspector observes for the designer or decides during driving, whom to contact and send records to, what reports are required, and how to inform the contractor of deviations without directing the work.
sections.body: 18.3 Review of Project Plans and Specifications (p. 451). The first task is a thorough review of plans and specifications for piles: all equipment and procedures, any indicator or static and/or dynamic test program, the preliminary driving criteria and how test results adjust them for hammer performance and soils; ask the specification's originator for clarification. The inspector should know whether they observe and report to the foundation designer or have direct decision responsibility during test and/or production driving; whom to contact or ask when something goes wrong; to whom driving records and daily reports go; what monitoring reports are required during and after the work; and how to inform the contractor of deviations from the contract without directing the contractor's work.
key_points: Review plans and specifications, test program and preliminary driving criteria first
Know whether the inspector observes or decides during driving
Know whom to contact, where records go, and what reports are required
Inform the contractor of deviations without directing the work
sections.applicability: The inspector's review of project documents before driving.

sections.title: Inspection of Piles Prior to and During Installation
sections.summary: Pile checklists differ by type; obtain the certificate of compliance and compare it with the specifications; combine the pile type checklist (18.5) with the hammer type checklist (18.7) for a project inspection list.
sections.body: 18.5 Inspection of Piles Prior to and During Installation (p. 452). Checklists differ by pile type but share some items. Specifications generally require a certificate of compliance, which the inspector obtains from the contractor and compares with the requirements. Sections 18.5.1 to 18.5.4 cover the major pile types and 18.7 the major hammer types; combining the project's pile and hammer checklists gives a detailed inspection list.
key_points: Obtain and check the certificate of compliance against the specifications
Project inspection list = pile type checklist (18.5) + hammer type checklist (18.7)
sections.applicability: Pile-type checklists for accepting piles before and during driving.

sections.title: Timber Piles
sections.summary: Timber piles (ASTM D25): specified species; minimum length, toe and butt sizes, butt cut square; acceptable spiral grain and knots; straightness; pressure treatment; banding; properly attached shoes; splices only if allowed.
sections.body: 18.5.1 Timber Piles (pp. 452 to 453). Round timber pile details are sometimes referenced to ASTM D25; check: (a) specified species; (b) minimum length and correct toe and butt sizes, butt cut square with the axis; (c) acceptable spiral grain twist and knots; (d) acceptable straightness; (e) pressure treatment as specified; (f) banding of butts and/or toes as in Chapter 16; (g) specified steel shoes properly attached (Chapter 16); (h) splices, if allowed, meeting requirements.
key_points: Species, length, toe and butt sizes per specification (ASTM D25)
Spiral grain, knots and straightness acceptable; pressure treated
Bands and shoes properly attached; splices only if allowed
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for timber piles.

sections.title: Precast Concrete Piles
sections.summary: Precast concrete: at the casting yard check forms, spiral and prestressing steel, splice and toe hardware alignment, concrete and curing, prestress transfer, handling; on site check length, section and strength or age, shipping damage, storage on blocking, lifting with cables at designated points (never chain slings), freedom in the helmet, no cracks or spalls.
sections.body: 18.5.2 Precast Concrete Piles (pp. 453 to 454). Agencies often inspect casting, or require a certificate of compliance. Casting yard items: (a) form geometry; (b) spiral reinforcing and prestressing strand dimensions, quantity, quality and certificate; (c) splice or embedded toe connection details (dowels) per approved details and cast within axial alignment tolerance; (d) concrete mix, slump, strength and curing; (e) prestressing forces and procedures including release time related to transfer strength; (f) handling, storage and minimum curing before stripping. Site items: (a) specified length and section, minimum waiting period or strength before driving, site splices to specification; (b) no shipping or unloading damage (sized, tensioned slings on lifting hooks; check for cracks or spalls); (c) storage above ground on blocking, straight, without undue bending; (d) proper, safe lifting into the leads with cables looped around the pile, never chain slings, no frayed cables, single pick-up for short piles, two or more designated points for long piles; (e) pile free to twist and move laterally in the helmet; (f) no noticeable cracks in the leads or during driving, no spalling at the top or near splices.
key_points: Casting yard: forms, strands, splice/toe hardware, concrete, prestress transfer, handling
Minimum age or concrete strength before driving
Lift with cables at designated pick-up points; never chain slings
Pile free to twist in the helmet; no cracks or spalls
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for precast and prestressed concrete piles.

sections.title: Steel H-Piles
sections.summary: Steel H-piles: specified grade, length and section; shoes as specified; proprietary or full penetration splices with aligned sections, properly welded; flanges oriented as on the plans (bending resistance differs by axis); no head damage.
sections.body: 18.5.3 Steel H-Piles (p. 455). On site: (a) specified steel grade, length and section/weight; (b) toe shoes as specified (Chapter 16); (c) proprietary splices or full penetration groove welds as specified, with sections well aligned before splicing; (d) splices and toe attachments properly welded; (e) flanges oriented as on the plans, since lateral bending resistance is considerably greater in the direction perpendicular to the flanges; (f) no observable damage including head deformation.
key_points: Specified grade, length and section; shoes as specified
Sections aligned before splicing; welds proper
Flange orientation per plans (bending resistance differs by axis)
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for steel H-piles.

sections.title: Steel Pipe Piles
sections.summary: Steel pipe piles: specified grade, length, wall thickness, seamless or spiral welded; closure plates or conical points (closed end) or cutting shoes (open end) properly welded; aligned splices; no head damage; inspect closed end pipes for damage or water before concreting.
sections.body: 18.5.4 Steel Pipe Piles (pp. 455 to 456). On site: (a) specified grade, length, minimum wall thickness, seamless or spiral welded; (b) driven open or closed end as specified, closed ends with closure plates or conical points of correct size properly welded, open ends with properly welded cutting shoes; (c) sections aligned before splicing, splices or full penetration welds as specified (Chapter 16); (d) no observable damage including head deformation; after installation inspect closed end pipes visually for damage or water before filling with concrete.
key_points: Specified grade, length, wall thickness; seamless or spiral welded
Closure plates, conical points or cutting shoes properly welded
Inspect closed end pipes for damage or water before concreting
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for steel pipe piles.

sections.title: Inspection of Driving Equipment
sections.summary: Before driving check: approved hammer and power source, stroke and energy measuring means (OED stroke chart or device, CED bounce gauge calibration and chart, hydraulic energy display); hammer cushion material, size and thickness; helmet fit and weight; concrete pile cushion (wave equation thickness, at least 4 in., new each pile, replace at half thickness, 1,000 to 2,000 blows); penetration aids; leads with a pile gate.
sections.body: 18.6 Inspection of Driving Equipment (pp. 456 to 461). The driving system (crane, leads, hammer, hammer cushion, helmet, and pile cushion for concrete) is checked for conformity before installation. 1 Hammer: approved make and model; single acting air/steam with proper power source and stroke; double acting or differential with proper source, pressure and volume; open end diesels with a stroke chart or electronic blow-rate stroke device; closed end diesels with a calibrated bounce chamber gauge and pressure-energy chart; hydraulic hammers with energy or impact velocity display. 2 Hammer cushion of approved material, size and thickness, fitting the helmet snugly, not excessively deformed; some air/steam hammers need a set cushion plus striker thickness for valve timing; check before driving and periodically on large projects, measuring cushion thickness and diameter, cushion pot and striker plate (Figures 18-3, 18-4). 3 Helmet fits the pile: loose enough to avoid torsion and bending, aligned, roughly pile-sized (spacers discouraged but allowed if concentric), critical for precast concrete; record helmet weight for wave equation (heavier reduces transfer). 4 Pile cushion for concrete piles: wave equation thickness, at least 4 in., new, not water soaked, for every pile (a 22 in. plywood cushion in Figures 18-5, 18-6 leaves little helmet depth); replace before compression over half, burning or charring; wood lasts about 1,000 to 2,000 blows; hard driving may need more than one per pile. 5 Predrilling, jetting or spudding equipment as permitted, depths carefully controlled since going deeper reduces resistance. 6 Leads conforming to the specification; poor alignment reduces energy and raises bending and contact stresses, especially at end of driving; require a centering pile gate. Note: keep the pile and driving equipment data form (like Figure 15-50) in the project files even without wave equation, and use it to compare proposed and actual equipment.
key_points: Hammer: approved make/model with the required stroke or energy measuring means
Hammer cushion: approved material, size and thickness; measure before driving
Helmet fits loosely but aligned; record helmet weight
Concrete pile cushion: >= 4 in., new each pile, replace at half thickness (1,000 to 2,000 blows)
Control predrilling, jetting or spudding depths
Leads with a centering pile gate; keep the equipment data form on file

sections.applicability: Inspecting pile driving equipment before driving.

sections.title: Inspection of Driving Equipment During Installation
sections.summary: Blow count depends on hammer performance as well as soil resistance, so the inspector must confirm the hammer performs properly before accepting a criterion; hammers of identical rating, even identical models, drive differently (friction, valve timing, hoses, fuel, rings, maintenance).
sections.body: 18.7 Inspection of Driving Equipment During Installation (pp. 461 to 462). Monitoring assures piles meet the driving criteria undamaged. Criteria are often a minimum blow count, which depends on hammer performance: higher energy and force give lower counts, lower give higher, and high counts may reflect soil resistance or a poorly performing hammer, so the inspector must check the hammer to be sure the criterion and nominal resistance are achieved. Do not assume the hammer is in good condition; two hammer types of identical rated energy will not give the same blow count, and even two of the same make and model may differ through friction, valve timing, air hose type, length and condition, fuel type and amount, ring condition and maintenance. Learn the hammer's operation (Chapter 15; manufacturers and suppliers); the checklists in 18.7.1 to 18.7.9 summarize key issues.
key_points: High blow counts may reflect soil resistance or a poorly performing hammer
Identically rated hammers, even identical models, drive differently
Confirm hammer performance before relying on the driving criterion
sections.applicability: Why and how hammers are inspected during pile installation.

sections.title: Drop Hammers
sections.summary: Drop hammers: confirm ram weight (from volume x 492 lb/ft3 if needed); free fall in greased guides; maintain the stroke (low reduces energy, high risks damage); helmet seated and aligned; hoist line spooling freely (catching the ram early loses energy and loads the crane).
sections.body: 18.7.1 Drop Hammers (p. 462). (a) Determine or confirm ram weight, calculable from ram volume and steel density of 492 lb/ft3; (b) leads with enough tolerance or greased guides so the ram falls without binding; (c) maintain the desired stroke: low strokes reduce energy, excessive strokes raise stresses and may damage the pile; (d) helmet seated and hammer and pile aligned; (e) hoist line spooling out freely during the drop and at impact: drag reduces energy, and catching the ram too early also transmits energy into line, boom and hoist, a maintenance and safety problem.
key_points: Confirm ram weight (volume x 492 lb/ft3)
Maintain the desired stroke; excessive strokes risk pile damage
Hoist line must spool freely; early catching loses energy
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for drop hammers.

sections.title: Single Acting Air/Steam Hammers
sections.summary: Single acting air/steam: confirm ram weight and labels; adequate supply pressure and volume (rated plus hose losses), hoses, lubricator; slide bar and cams; greased guides; cushion plus striker thickness for valve timing; tight keys; slack hoist line; compare blows per minute with specifications; reduce flow if racking; warranties over 10 blows/in.; Table 18-2 problems; Figure 18-8 inspection form.
sections.body: 18.7.2 Single Acting Air/Steam Hammers (pp. 463 to 467). (a) Confirm ram weight (492 lb/ft3) and record make, model and serial number; (b) supply of adequate pressure and flow, hoses' number, length, diameter and condition per manufacturer guidelines, hose blown through before attaching, lubricator filled; compressor or boiler pressure equal to rated plus hose losses and steady (Figure 18-7 discharge pressure dial); (c) slide bar and cams not worn (some have dual cams for two strokes switched from the ground); measure the stroke; (d) columns or guides, piston rod and slide bar greased; (e) total hammer cushion plus striker plate thickness matching manufacturer and helmet cavity for valve timing, checked before placing the helmet and by cam-valve position or ram-base gap; (f) helmet seated, alignment kept; (g) ram and column keys tight; (h) hoist line slack, weight on the pile, leads always used; (i) blows per minute near end of driving (stopwatch or saximeter) compared with specifications: slow rates imply short stroke (pressure, volume, hose, lubrication) or improper valve timing (cushion thickness, worn parts); erratic operation from cushion thickness, lubrication, foreign material, valves or loose keys; (j) if rising stroke strikes the upper assembly and lifts the hammer ('racking'), reduce flow gradually, not so much that stroke falls; (k) some manufacturers void warranties above 10 blows per inch beyond short periods, so prolonged hard driving may need a larger hammer or stiffer pile; (l) Table 18-2 (after Williams Earth Sciences 1995) problems and indicators: trip mechanism malfunction (erratic rates, valve sticking), wrong cushion stack height (erratic rates), compressor pressure or volume wrong (blow rate off specification), kinked supply line, icing (ice crystals at exhaust), no lubricant (erratic), worn air chest packing (slow ram, air leaks), worn nylon slide bar, ungreased columns. Figure 18-8: inspector's form for single and differential acting air/steam hammers (driving system objects, manufacturer requirements, observed condition; final driving observations to compare with the wave equation; copy to design and construction staff).
key_points: Supply pressure = rated pressure plus hose losses, steady during driving
Cushion plus striker plate thickness sets valve timing
Compare blows per minute with manufacturer specifications
Racking: reduce air flow gradually, not enough to cut the stroke
Table 18-2: common air/steam hammer problems and indicators; Figure 18-8 inspection form

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Air/Steam Hammers
tables.description: Air/steam hammer problems and indicators: air trip malfunction (erratic rates, valve sticking); wrong cushion stack height (erratic rates); compressor pressure or volume (blow rate off specification); kinked air line (visible); moisture icing (ice at exhaust ports); no lubricant (erratic rates); worn air chest packing (slow ram, air leaking); worn nylon slide bar and ungreased columns (visible).

sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for single acting air and steam hammers.

sections.title: Double Acting or Differential Air/ Steam Hammers
sections.summary: Double acting or differential air/steam: as single acting, but supply pressure and volume are critical since about half the rated energy comes from downstroke pressure; record starting and final pressure and compare with the energy rating; keep pressure as full as possible with lift-off imminent; Figure 18-9 form for enclosed double acting hammers.
sections.body: 18.7.3 Double Acting or Differential Air/ Steam Hammers (pp. 468 to 471). Items as for single acting hammers (ram weight, labels, hoses, lubricator, slide bar and cams, grease, cushion plus striker thickness for valve timing, alignment, keys, slack hoist line, blows per minute, warranties above 10 blows per inch, Table 18-2), with: (b) adequate supply is extremely important since approximately half the rated energy comes from pressure on the ram during the downstroke; record the starting pressure; (j) if racking occurs reduce flow gradually, which reduces energy as the pressure also acts on the downstroke; record the final pressure; do not restrict so much that the stroke falls too; for optimum performance keep the flow as full as possible with lift-off imminent; (l) compare the final pressure with the manufacturer's energy rating at that pressure. Figure 18-9 is the inspector's form for enclosed double acting air/steam hammers, used periodically with the driving log, with final driving observations for comparison with the wave equation.
key_points: About half the rated energy comes from downstroke pressure: supply is critical
Record starting and final pressure; compare final pressure with the energy rating
Keep flow as full as possible with lift-off imminent
Figure 18-9: inspection form for enclosed double acting hammers

figures.title: Inspector’s form for enclosed double acting air/steam hammers

sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for double acting and differential air and steam hammers.

sections.title: Single Acting Diesel Hammers
sections.summary: Single acting diesel: make and model; exhaust ports open; recoil dampener condition and thickness; lubrication (impact block every half hour); determine stroke by saximeter or h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 (Eq. 18-1), never a jump stick; low stroke from fuel setting, injector or worn rings (bounce test); watch for pre-ignition (check by dynamic testing); Table 18-3 problems; Figure 18-12 form.
sections.body: 18.7.4 Single Acting Diesel Hammers (pp. 471 to 476). (a) Correct make and model, labels recorded; (b) exhaust ports open, plugs removed; (c) recoil dampener condition and thickness: too thin reduces stroke, too thick or a cylinder not resting on it can let the ram blow out the top; (d) grease nipples lubricated, impact block typically every half hour; (e) ram visible between blows showing uniform lubrication and rotation; (f) determine stroke, especially at end of driving or beginning of restrike; a 'jump stick' is a safety hazard; a saximeter measures time between blows; h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 (Eq. 18-1; h stroke ft, bpm blows per minute), possibly corrected for batter; also observe ram rings against the manufacturer's chart; (g) stroke should rise with blow count; a short final stroke may be lack of fuel: check the pump setting (stepped, continuously variable or pressure pump; Figures 18-10, 18-11), clean fuel and injectors; (h) low strokes from worn piston or anvil rings: with fuel off, a dropped ram should bounce several times; (i) pre-ignition burns fuel before impact, leaving less energy and raising the blow count, falsely indicating high resistance; it follows long driving or low flash point fuel; suspect it if cold-hammer piles drive deeper or blow counts drop after breaks; dynamic testing is preferable for checking; (j) cushion plus striker thickness for some diesels; (k) alignment; (l) slack hoist line, leads used; (m) warranties above 10 blows per inch; (n) Table 18-3 (after Williams Earth Sciences 1995): water in fuel or combustion chamber (hollow sound, white smoke), clogged fuel lines (no or little gray smoke), pump or injector faults (inconsistent strokes, gray or black smoke), low oil or oil pump fault (low blow rate), worn rings (low strokes), broken trip (pawl does not engage or lift), overheating (paint and oil on fins burn, sound changes). Figure 18-12: inspector's form for single acting diesels.
key_points: Recoil dampener: too thin reduces stroke; too thick risks ram blow-out
Stroke by saximeter or h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 (Eq. 18-1); never a jump stick
Short stroke: check fuel setting, injectors, ring compression (bounce test)
Pre-ignition raises blow count falsely; check with dynamic testing
Table 18-3: diesel hammer problems and indicators; Figure 18-12 form

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Single Acting Diesel Hammers
tables.description: Single acting diesel problems and indicators: water in fuel or combustion chamber (hollow sound, white smoke); clogged fuel lines (no or little gray smoke); fuel pump or injector malfunction (inconsistent strokes, gray or black smoke); low oil or oil pump malfunction (blow rate low); worn piston rings (low strokes); broken tripping device (pawl does not engage or lift); overheating (paint and oil on fins burn, sound changes).

sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for single acting (open end) diesel hammers.

sections.title: Double Acting Diesel Hammers
sections.summary: Double acting diesel: as single acting, plus always measure bounce chamber pressure (external gauge, chart for the hose size and length) especially at end of driving or restrike; reduce fuel to keep lift-off imminent; a gauge not reading maximum pressure at imminent lift-off is out of calibration or the tank needs draining; Table 18-4; Figure 18-14 form.
sections.body: 18.7.5 Double Acting Diesel Hammers (pp. 476 to 481). Items as for single acting diesels (make, model, exhaust ports, recoil dampener (too thick causes lift-off), lubrication every half hour, ram lubrication seen through the exhaust port or trip slot after stopping, rings, pre-ignition, cushion thickness, alignment, slack hoist line, warranties), with: (f) always measure bounce chamber pressure, especially at end of driving or restrike, as an indirect measure of equivalent stroke or energy, usually by an external gauge on a hose (Figure 18-13), compared with the manufacturer's chart for that hose size and length, possibly corrected for batter; (g) stroke and bounce pressure should rise with resistance; low values at final driving may be lack of fuel (continuously variable pumps), dirty fuel or injectors; (h) in hard driving, if the cylinder weight cannot balance the bounce pressure the hammer lifts off, so the operator reduces fuel, ideally keeping lift-off imminent; the gauge should then read the maximum pressure for the hose length, or it is out of calibration or the tank needs draining; (o) Table 18-4 (after Williams Earth Sciences 1995) as Table 18-3 plus oil build-up in the bounce chamber (not visible from outside). Figure 18-14: inspector's form for double acting diesels.
key_points: Always measure bounce chamber pressure, especially at end of driving or restrike
Use the manufacturer's chart for the hose size and length
Reduce fuel so lift-off is imminent; gauge should then read maximum pressure
Table 18-4: double acting diesel problems; Figure 18-14 form

figures.title: Typical external bounce chamber pressure gauge
Inspector’s form for double acting diesel hammers

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Double Acting Diesel Hammers
tables.description: Double acting diesel problems and indicators: as for single acting diesels plus oil build-up in the bounce chamber (not visible from outside).

sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for double acting (closed end) diesel hammers.

sections.title: Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers
sections.summary: Single acting hydraulic: confirm ram weight (rams may be hollow or lead filled); adequate power supply and hoses (no tight bends); clean, filters; correct speed and pressure, warm up; measure visible strokes; grease; cushion thickness; slack hoist line; blows per minute; reduce flow if racking (sensors may shut down); Table 18-5; Figure 18-15 form.
sections.body: 18.7.6 Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers (pp. 482 to 484). (a) Confirm ram weight (492 lbs/ft3, though some rams are hollow or lead filled) and record labels; (b) power supply pressure and flow, hoses without leaks and not bent below the recommended radius; (c) clean, free of dirt and water, filters unblocked, built-in diagnostics; (d) power pack at correct speed and pressure, hammer warmed up, pack not turned off immediately after driving; (e) measure stroke where the ram is observable (impossible for enclosed rams); (f) guides and piston rod greased; (g) cushion plus striker thickness where applicable; (h) alignment; (i) slack hoist line, leads used; (j) slower blow rates at full stroke may mean excessive friction or wrong power supply; (k) racking: reduce flow gradually (many hammers shut down automatically), keeping the correct stroke; (l) warranties above 10 blows per inch; (m) Table 18-5 (after Williams Earth Sciences 1995): hoses caught in leads (visible), leaking fittings (dripping fluid), electrical connections or sensors (erratic performance). Figure 18-15: inspector's form for single acting hydraulic hammers.
key_points: Confirm ram weight (rams may be hollow or lead filled)
Power supply speed and pressure; hoses not bent below recommended radius
Measure stroke where the ram is visible; compare blow rate at full stroke
Table 18-5: hydraulic hammer problems; Figure 18-15 form

figures.title: Inspector’s form for single acting hydraulic hammers

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers
tables.description: Single acting hydraulic problems and indicators: hoses caught in leads (visible); leaking fittings (fluid dripping); electrical connections and sensors (erratic performance).

sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for single acting hydraulic hammers.

sections.title: Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers
sections.summary: Double acting hydraulic: as single acting, plus record accumulator pre-charge; verify the ram weight in the hammer's computer and constantly record the measured impact velocity, stroke or energy (the most important check); energy readout mandatory as rams are enclosed; document anvil or cushioning; Table 18-6 (nitrogen caps); Figure 18-17 form.
sections.body: 18.7.7 Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers (pp. 485 to 488). Items as for single acting hydraulic hammers, with: (d) check and record pre-charge pressures or accumulators; (e) built-in sensors give ram velocity before impact, converted to kinetic energy or equivalent stroke: verify the correct ram weight in the hammer's computer and constantly monitor and record the result (some print it with depth and blow count), the most important hammer check for these hammers (readout panel Figure 18-16); (f) most are fully enclosed, so stroke cannot be observed and working energy readouts are mandatory; (g) most use steel ram on steel anvil without striker plate or cushion (one uses an aluminum stack; concrete pile models a synthetic anvil): document the anvil or cushioning and dimensions. Table 18-6 (double acting hydraulic hammers with nitrogen caps): crossed hoses or wrong accumulator pressure (jumping hoses), cap pressure too high (hammer jumping), low oil (erratic), valve malfunction (erratic or no operation), control cable disconnected (inoperable, panel bulb not lit), plus the Table 18-5 items. Figure 18-17: inspector's form for hydraulic hammers.
key_points: Verify ram weight in the hammer computer; record measured velocity/energy constantly
Energy readout mandatory: enclosed rams cannot be observed
Record accumulator pre-charge; document anvil or cushion

sections.title: Resonant Hammers
sections.summary: Resonant hammers: make and model; power supply and hoses; clean, filters; correct speed and pressure, warm up; record the resonant frequency; effective clamps; hoist line slack enough for penetration (tight for extraction); leads optional.
sections.body: 18.7.8 Resonant Hammers (p. 489). (a) Make and model meet specifications, labels recorded; (b) power supply pressure and flow, hoses without leaks or tight bends; (c) clean, filters unblocked, diagnostics; (d) check and record power supply speed and pressure, warm up, do not shut down immediately after driving; (e) record the resonant vibrating frequency; (f) hydraulic clamps in good working order; (g) hoist line slack enough to allow penetration with the weight mainly on the pile (excess tension retards penetration), tight for extraction; leads may or may not be used.
key_points: Record the resonant vibrating frequency
Hydraulic clamps in good working order
Hoist line slack for driving, tight for extraction
sections.applicability: Inspection checklist for resonant hammers.

sections.title: Vibratory Hammers
sections.summary: Vibratory hammers: as resonant hammers, recording the vibrating frequency if available; effective clamps; hoist line slack for driving, tight for extraction; leads rarely used.
sections.body: 18.7.9 Vibratory Hammers (pp. 489 to 490). (a) Make and model meet specifications, labels recorded; (b) power supply pressure and flow, hoses without leaks or tight bends; (c) clean, filters unblocked, diagnostics; (d) check and record power supply speed and pressure, warm up, do not shut down immediately after driving; (e) record the vibrating frequency if available; (f) hydraulic clamps in good working order; (g) hoist line slack enough for penetration (excess tension retards it), tight for extraction; leads are rarely used.
key_points: Record the vibrating frequency if available
Hydraulic clamps in good working order
Hoist line slack for driving, tight for extraction; leads rarely used

sections.title: Inspection of Test or Indicator Piles
sections.summary: Test or indicator piles set criteria for all production piles and offer the largest savings; small conservative jobs may have none, so thorough inspection is the only assurance; mid-size jobs use a static test or a few dynamic tests on early piles; large jobs test across the site. Settle 14 questions (who locates, stops, accepts, authorizes production) before driving.
sections.body: 18.8 Inspection of Test or Indicator Piles (pp. 490 to 492). Most projects verify design and resistance by testing selected piles, the size and cost dictating type and number; the inspector may coordinate the program. Small foundations designed conservatively may have no test piles; all piles are production piles installed in a day or two, inspection is the only assurance, and problems (very low blow counts, refusal above scour depth, excessive lengths) must be reported quickly. Small to mid-size projects may have a single static test (Chapter 9) or a few dynamic tests (Chapter 10) during driving (hammer performance, stresses) and/or restrike (resistance), by knowledgeable personnel, usually on early piles to verify or adjust criteria. Larger projects use multiple test piles across the site, at the start (e.g., indicator piles for concrete pile order lengths) or in stages. Test piles are the most critical part: criteria apply to all production piles, the largest savings arise (e.g., shorter piles), and test pile problems recur in production, so resolve them fast and report precisely and promptly. Before test driving, ideally at a preconstruction meeting, answer: who determines test pile locations; the test driving criteria; who stops driving; who decides indicator pile depth; who checks cutoff and heave; who judges static or dynamic results; who requires more tests or changes to procedures or equipment; what documentation and by whom; who produces production criteria and how quickly; who authorizes production driving and when; and whether production piles may be driven ahead of criteria, and at whose risk.
key_points: Test piles set the criteria for all production piles; largest savings arise here
Small conservative jobs may have no test piles: inspection is the only assurance
Report problems (low blow counts, refusal above scour, excess length) quickly
Settle who decides locations, termination, acceptance and production start beforehand
sections.applicability: Inspecting test and indicator pile programs.

sections.title: Inspection of Production Piles
sections.summary: Check every production pile (17 items); verify hammer by blow rate, stroke, bounce pressure or energy monitor; ignore the first 100 blows after a cushion change and do not change cushions near final driving; keep stresses in limits; avoid over 10 blows/in.; check damage; drive displacement groups center-out or side to side, nearest structures first; surveys within 400 ft; warm hammer for restrikes; Table 18-7 problems and solutions.
sections.body: 18.9 Inspection of Production Piles (pp. 493 to 502). The inspector applies the test program to every production pile, covering pile and splice quality, hammer operation and cushion replacement, integrity, completion (concrete filling) and unusual events, with complete timely documentation. Check each pile: type, size, length, strength; location, tolerance, orientation; splices; toe protection; plumbness; hammer working; hammer cushion; pile cushion and its replacement; criteria met; unusual driving; heave; cutoff elevation; visible damage; pipe piles inspected before and filled with specified concrete, sampled; voided piles cleaned; integrity questions resolved; documentation complete and submitted. Verify hammers by blows per minute, visible air/steam and hydraulic strokes, saximeter or Eq. 18-1 for open end diesels, bounce pressure for closed end diesels, and built-in energy monitors (mandatory on double acting hydraulic hammers), with the hammer inspection form. Manufactured hammer cushions last up to 200 hours; plywood pile cushions about 1000 to 2000 blows, replaced at half thickness or burning; no cushion changes near final driving, and blow counts for resistance only after the first 100 blows on a new cushion (a new cushion inflates the count). Inspect splices; keep stresses within limits by dynamic testing or wave equation, adjusting stroke or cushions; avoid driving above 10 blows per inch; compare records of adjacent piles and test suspected damage by high strain or low strain integrity testing (Chapter 10); check closed end pipes for water and soil, use high slump small aggregate concrete, inspect with a light or mirror. Drive displacement groups from the center outward or from one side to the other (Figure 18-18, sequences 1 to 3), never outside to center (trapped, compacted soil); near structures or utilities drive the nearest piles first and work away (e.g., near bascule bridges). Woods (1997): vibration damage is uncommon beyond one pile length, but vibration-induced settlement of loose clean sands can matter up to 1300 ft; preconstruction surveys within 400 ft, or within 0.25 times the square root of hammer energy (ft-lbs) in feet; fresh concrete risk unclear. Warm hammers with about twenty blows before restrikes and record blows per inch. Table 18-7 problems and solutions: refusal above minimum penetration (wave equation, hammer checks, dynamic measurements for pre-ignition, preadmission, soft cushion, strong soil, relaxation, large quakes, high damping); driving much deeper (restrike, check hammer, longer or more piles); abrupt blow count drop on bearing piles (toe damage: reduce energy, inspect inside, dynamic test); low blow counts (damage below grade, splices); heave or lateral movement (redrive, resequence, predrill); alignment or location tolerance (pile gate, template, fixed leads; survey and consult); shallow obstructions within 10 ft (excavate, spud or predrill); deep obstructions (redesign, reduce resistance); complete or partial horizontal cracks in concrete piles (tension: cushion, stroke, heavier ram, quakes; alignment); head spalling, steel head deformation or timber mushrooming (stress check, cushion, helmet, energy; no resistance from blow counts with damaged heads).
key_points: Check each production pile against 17 items, with complete documentation
Verify hammer by blow rate, stroke (Eq. 18-1), bounce pressure or energy monitor
No cushion change near final driving; ignore first 100 blows on a new cushion
Avoid driving above 10 blows/in.; keep stresses within limits
Displacement groups: center outward or side to side; nearest a structure first
Preconstruction surveys within about 400 ft; sand settlement possible to 1300 ft
Table 18-7: common installation problems and possible solutions

tables.title: Common Pile Installation Problems and Possible Solutions
tables.description: Problems and solutions: refusal above minimum penetration (wave equation drivability, hammer checks, dynamic measurements: pre-ignition, preadmission, soft cushion, or soil strength, relaxation, quakes, damping); driving deeper than estimated (wave equation, restrike, deeper or added piles); abrupt decrease in blow count on bearing piles (toe damage likely; reduce stroke or change hammer or section; inspect inside or test); blow count lower than expected (damage below grade, splice failure); heave or lateral movement of installed piles (redrive, change sequence, predrill); out of alignment or location tolerance (pile gate, template, fixed leads; survey as-built); shallow obstructions (excavate if within 10 ft; else spud or predrill); obstructions at depth (reduce resistance, added piles); concrete cracks in easy driving (cushion or stroke), hard driving (heavier ram, quakes), partial cracks (alignment, bending); spalling at head (cushion); steel head deforms and timber head mushrooms (helmet, evenness, banding; no acceptance from those blow counts).

sections.applicability: Inspecting production pile installation.

sections.title: Driving Records and Reports
sections.summary: Pile driving records (Figure 18-19) list project, structure, times, contractor, hammer and stroke, cushions and helmet, pile data and elevations, blows per foot with the final foot in blows per inch, lengths, comments and the inspector's signature; they underpin payment, engineering decisions and claims; also keep daily inspection reports (Figure 18-20).
sections.body: 18.10 Driving Records and Reports (pp. 502 to 505). Records vary by organization (typical record Figure 18-19); most list: project number, name and location; structure number; date and times (start, stop, interruptions); contractor; hammer make, model, ram weight and energy rating, with stroke and operating speed whenever changed; hammer cushion and helmet weight; pile cushion and depth where changed; pile location, type, size and length; pile number matching the layout; ground, cutoff and final penetration elevations and embedded length; blows per foot with the final foot normally in blows per inch; optional graph; cutoff, in-ground and order lengths; comments including reasons for interruptions; inspector's signature and title. Records form the basis for payment and foundation adequacy decisions and weigh heavily in claims; sloppy records encourage claims and raise costs, good ones lower cost and keep schedule. A daily inspection report (Figure 18-20) records equipment, work accomplished and progress.
key_points: Driving records: hammer, stroke, cushions, pile data, elevations, blow counts, comments
Final foot normally recorded in blows per inch
Records underpin payment, engineering decisions and claims
Daily inspection reports record equipment, work and progress

sections.title: Safety
sections.summary: Inspector safety: plan an escape route while piles are lifted (a 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft away); avoid suspended loads, the area behind the crane and in front of the pile; keep away from the hammer (falling parts, breaking piles, line failure); pre-mark 1 in. increments instead of marking near the hammer; wear protective equipment.
sections.body: 18.11 Safety (p. 506). Lifting and positioning a pile under the hammer is among the most dangerous operations: a 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft from its location, so plan an escape route beforehand. Avoid the area beneath suspended loads and behind the crane, and watch for crane movement or swing. Keep the recording position a sufficient distance away, not immediately in front of the pile: heavy pieces can fall from hammer or helmet, concrete and timber piles can break suddenly, long steel piles buckle, a sudden loss of resistance can break the hammer line, and damaged concrete heads shed pieces. Do not stand beneath the hammer marking the pile every 10 or 20 blows; mark 1 in. increments over the anticipated final penetration before driving. Wear a hard hat, ear and eye protection, steel toed boots, safety vest, fall harness and life jacket as conditions dictate, and review site, state and federal rules.
key_points: Plan an escape route when piles are lifted (a 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft away)
Avoid suspended loads, behind the crane and in front of the pile
Pre-mark 1 in. increments instead of marking the pile under the hammer
Wear protective equipment as job conditions dictate
sections.applicability: Safety of the pile driving inspector.
